General Napoleon

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: This is a picture, not a game: three small triangles stand on the sides of a big one, and their corner lines meet at one spot.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a corner and use the arrow keys. Move the sliders to change the small triangles, and tick Show names to see the points.
Look for the math

Move a corner of the big triangle and the three small triangles swing around, yet three lines still pass through one spot. That is the claim on the old cut-the-knot page, which still embeds its Java applet; the picture here is the same construction drawn with SVG. The applet's name mentions Napoleon, but the statement it illustrates is a generalization of Kiepert's theorem.

What the two sliders choose

On side AB the applet puts K near A and L near B; on BC it puts P near B and Q near C; on CA it puts M near C and N near A. The first slider sets how far L, Q and N sit from their other end, and the second does the same for K, P and M. In the page's barycentric coordinates this says AK/AB = BP/BC = CM/CA on every side. When the two slider numbers add to 1, each pair is made of isotomic conjugates: for instance AK = LB. That is the hypothesis of the page's theorem.

Three matching small triangles

Each tip is found by turning the far end of the side about each base point by the chosen angle, and taking where the two turned lines cross. Both base angles of the little triangle are therefore the same, so KLC', PQA' and MNB' are isosceles triangles with the same apex angle. Their bases have matching fractions of the big triangle's sides, so the three little triangles are similar and point the same way. At an angle of 0 or 90 degrees the two lines are parallel and there is no tip; the applet draws nothing there, and neither does this page.

The claim, checked

The page says: using KL, MN and PQ as bases, form similar and similarly oriented isosceles triangles KLC', MNB' and PQA'; then AA', BB', CC' are concurrent. The logic test confirms this over hundreds of triangles and every slider value in the applet's range whenever the two slider numbers add to 1: the three pairwise meeting points agree to within a drawing error of about 0.0002 pixels. It also finds counterexamples when they do not add to 1, so the isotomic condition really is needed. The applet itself switches off its meeting dot outside the band 0.99 .. 1.01 and draws only the apex-to-corner lines; this page does the same.

Why a meeting point exists

The page proves it by showing that BA' and BC' are isogonal conjugates at B, and the same at A and C. Similar triangles give equal angles at the base points, and equal lengths then force those mirror-image directions. A theorem of D. Gale turns three such isogonal pairs into one meeting point. Setting one slider to 0 and the other to 1 makes each base a whole side: that is Kiepert's theorem, whose meeting point traces a Kiepert hyperbola as the angle changes. The middle-thirds equilateral case studied by Garfunkel and Stahl is another special case.

Try putting both sliders at 0.50 and watch the bases shrink to nothing, then move them back so they add to 1 and see the green lines meet again.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
